pending_qa.q: What role did Bernardino de Mendoza play in the dispute over Drake's treasure?
pending_qa.r: Bernardino de Mendoza, Philip II's ambassador to Elizabeth's court, was described as a menacing, zealously Catholic figure who actively worked to subvert Elizabeth's regime. He demanded an audience to protest Drake's actions and sent Elizabeth a blunt warning — 'A war is easily begun, but not so soon ended' — but Elizabeth deflected him by demanding a full account of the Spanish invasion of Ireland before agreeing to meet him.

pending_qa.q: How did Elizabeth I manage to reward Drake without openly provoking Spain?
pending_qa.r: Elizabeth handled the situation through deliberate duplicity: she officially ordered Drake to register his treasure and send it to the Tower, while secretly allowing him to keep £10,000 and his crew to retain £14,000. She returned £30,000 to Spanish merchants who could prove legitimate claims in London but otherwise publicly declared that Drake had no charge to answer and dismissed Spanish allegations as lies.

pending_qa.q: What was the significance of Elizabeth I knighting Francis Drake on the Golden Hind at Deptford on 1 April 1581?
pending_qa.r: Knighting Drake was a bold and deliberately theatrical public statement, as Elizabeth was famously stingy with knighthoods and Drake was the grandson of a yeoman farmer — an almost unheard-of recipient of such an honour. The ceremony served multiple purposes: it burnished Elizabeth's image as Gloriana, rallied domestic public opinion, and sent a public signal to Spain about the strength of England's alliance with France, since a French envoy named Monsieur de Marchemont actually performed the dubbing.

pending_qa.q: Who were the 'Three Henries' (Trois Henri) in France during the late sixteenth century, and what did each represent?
pending_qa.r: The three factions in France were each led by a man named Henri: Henri of Navarre led the Huguenots and would eventually become Henri IV; Henri, Duke of Guise, led the ultra-Catholic League and was effectively the master of Paris and commander of the largest armies; and Henri III was the actual king of France, attempting to hold his kingdom together between these two extreme factions.

pending_qa.q: Why was the Duke of Guise a threat to both Elizabeth I and Mary Queen of Scots' enemies?
pending_qa.r: The Duke of Guise was cousin to Mary, Queen of Scots, which meant he could realistically aspire to the thrones of England and Scotland: if he deposed Elizabeth and married Mary, he would control both kingdoms. He was described as the darling of Catholic diehards in Paris, with a martial charisma enhanced by a visible saber scar gained in battle in 1575, and was rumoured to want to make himself king of France as well.

pending_qa.q: How did increased silver production in the Americas affect the balance of power between Spain and Protestant England?
pending_qa.r: Drake had discovered during his voyage that technological advances in South America were fuelling increased silver extraction from the great mines there, producing a growing flow of silver back to Spain. Philip II was using this silver to fund his armies in the Low Countries against Protestant rebels and to sustain his broader Cold War against Protestant England, which led Elizabeth to reason that she was entitled to use Spain's captured silver against him.

pending_qa.q: What happened to the Spanish military force in Ireland when Drake returned to England in 1580?
pending_qa.r: When Drake returned, a Spanish invasion force was still active in Ireland, with Catholic priests including two Jesuits also operating in England. By November 1580, however, the Spanish task force in Ireland had been crushed and wiped out at a place called Smerwick, which strengthened Elizabeth's position in her standoff with Mendoza.
